segments.flavor: the station ID — the signature
segments.text: Rupert: [gentle] Concert Hall. Every program note here is a chase, and every chase ends in music. Listen.

segments.flavor: the station ID — the radiator in B flat
segments.text:
Rupert: Concert Hall. The radiator in the east wall holds a steady B flat.
Rupert: The orchestra has decided to join it. Strings, please.

segments.flavor: the station ID — a composer runs out of time
segments.text:
Rupert: [serious] This is Concert Hall. Somewhere in the next hour, a composer runs out of time.
Rupert: We know how it ends. He finishes. Play it.

segments.flavor: the station ID — the dates are exact
segments.text:
Rupert: Concert Hall. The story is true, the dates are approximate, and the music is exact.
Hilde: The dates are not approximate. I am here. Begin.

segments.flavor: Rupert tells one ordinary biographical fact about a composer as a thriller — debts, deadlines, a chase — and lands on 'and then — silence'
segments.text:
Rupert: He owed a tailor for two coats. The finale was due. He wrote it on the bill.
Rupert: And then — silence. Then the finale. It starts now.

segments.flavor: Rupert tells one ordinary biographical fact about a composer as a thriller — debts, deadlines, a chase — and lands on 'and then — silence'
segments.text:
Rupert: He sold one sonata to three publishers in one week, and spelled his name differently each time.
Rupert: All three printed it. All three were right. Here is the sonata.

segments.flavor: back-announce {STREAM} as tonight's orchestra, with one line of program notes
segments.text:
Rupert: That was our orchestra, unhurried, in a hall with better acoustics than ours.
Rupert: The second movement was written for a friend who never heard it. More, in a moment.

segments.flavor: back-announce {STREAM} as tonight's orchestra, with one line of program notes
segments.text:
Rupert: That was tonight's orchestra, playing a wedding dance that the composer wrote for a funeral.
Rupert: Nobody noticed for a hundred years. We noticed tonight. The next one begins now.

segments.flavor: Rupert tells one ordinary biographical fact about a composer as a thriller — debts, deadlines, a chase — and lands on 'and then — silence'
segments.text:
Rupert: A young organist wanted to hear the greatest player alive, so he walked. Two hundred miles.
Hilde: On foot. In winter. With no promise the man would be at the keyboard.
Rupert: He stayed four months. His employers were furious. And then — silence.
Hilde: Then this. Listen to what he brought home.

segments.flavor: Hilde corrects one date or key signature with love; Rupert accepts the correction like a plot twist
segments.text:
Rupert: The piece we just heard sits in C minor, which is the key of storms and debts.
Hilde: E flat major, Rupert. With love. The storm is two pieces later.
Rupert: E flat. So the debts were paid. That changes the whole evening.
Hilde: It changes nothing. Play the next one.

segments.flavor: a fake ad for hearing aids, velvet seats or a subscription series, hushed sincere announcer grammar, rapid disclaimer from Hilde
segments.text:
Rupert: [gentle] A word about Velvetine, the cushion for the third hour of an opera.
Hilde: The third hour is when the seat becomes the subject of the evening.
Rupert: Velvetine is silent. It forgives. It asks nothing of your posture.
Hilde: Velvetine is not a cure for the plot. Back to the orchestra.

segments.flavor: Gus the night watchman weighs in on the last tempo; he thinks it rushed, and he has keys to find
segments.text:
Gus: Watchman. That last movement went by like a man late for a train.
Rupert: Gus, the marking is allegro vivace.
Gus: The marking has never carried a ring of keys down a dark corridor.
Hilde: [chuckle] The next piece is slow, Gus. Take the long way round.

segments.flavor: a fake ad — Larghetto lozenges, read solo
segments.text:
Rupert: Larghetto lozenges dissolve in complete silence, wrapped in soft paper, for the patron in row G with a cough.
Rupert: Larghetto does not treat the cough. It treats the wrapper only. Now, back to the andante.

segments.flavor: a fake ad — Quietleaf programmes, paper that does not rustle
segments.text:
Rupert: [gentle] Quietleaf prints the evening programme on paper that does not rustle.
Hilde: The page turns. Nobody turns with it.
Rupert: Every note, every date, every name, in type large enough to read in the dark.
Hilde: The dates are correct. I checked them myself, twice, with a candle.
Rupert: Quietleaf. The only sound in the hall should be the orchestra.
Hilde: Quietleaf paper is not suitable for paper aeroplanes, fans, or hats.
Rupert: Especially hats. The second half begins.

segments.flavor: a fake ad — Cadenza opera glasses
segments.text:
Rupert: Cadenza opera glasses bring the conductor's eyebrows to within a foot of your face.
Hilde: You will see the exact moment he decides to take the repeat.
Rupert: You will see the second oboe agree with him. Silently. Professionally.
Hilde: You will see a great deal of the harpist's shoes.
Rupert: Cadenza. Because the interesting part is never at the front.
Hilde: Cadenza is for the stage only, and the balcony has rules about this.
Rupert: It does. Eyes forward. The concerto continues.

segments.flavor: a fake ad — The Long Programme, a subscription series
segments.text:
Rupert: [serious] The Long Programme. Nine concerts. One seat. Your seat, from autumn to spring.
Hilde: The same seat every time. The same neighbour every time.
Rupert: By the fourth concert you will know his coat. By the sixth, his opinions.
Hilde: By the ninth you will have agreed about one slow movement and nothing else.
Rupert: That is a friendship. The Long Programme sells it in a single envelope.
Hilde: The Long Programme cannot move you away from him. We have tried, on your behalf.
Rupert: Nine nights. One envelope. The first of them starts with this.

segments.flavor: And Then — Silence — the copyist
segments.text:
Rupert: [serious] And then — silence. Tonight, the copyist.
Hilde: The most frightened man in the building, every time.
Rupert: The parts were still wet when the audience sat down. He carried them up the aisle.
Hilde: Second violins got their pages during the applause for the conductor.
Rupert: They sight-read a premiere. In public. For money.
Hilde: And it went perfectly, which is the part nobody believes.
Rupert: Listen to the piece that was still drying. Second violins, forgive them.

segments.flavor: And Then — Silence — the drum one bar early
segments.text:
Rupert: The timpanist counted one hundred and forty bars of rest.
Hilde: One hundred and forty-one. That is the whole story.
Rupert: He came in one bar early, alone, in a silent hall, on the loudest instrument there.
Hilde: [gasp] In front of the composer.
Rupert: In front of the composer, who stood up.
Hilde: And wrote it into the score the following morning. The early entry is now correct.
Rupert: Three hundred players since have played a mistake with total conviction.
Hilde: They have no idea. Listen for the drum, one bar too soon.

segments.flavor: And Then — Silence — the horn player on the ice
segments.text:
Rupert: Tonight on And Then — Silence, a horn player, a river, and a bridge that was gone.
Hilde: The bridge went in a flood. The premiere was across the water.
Rupert: He walked onto the ice at four in the afternoon with the horn on his back.
Hilde: The ice held. It had held for a month. It held for him.
Rupert: Halfway across, it spoke. One long crack, from bank to bank.
Hilde: [gasp] And he stopped.
Rupert: He did not stop. He was late.
Hilde: He arrived during the tuning, sat down, and played the solo cold.
Rupert: And then — silence, and then that solo. It is the one you know.
Hilde: Here it is, with the ice still in it.

segments.flavor: And Then — Silence — the flat harpsichord
segments.text:
Rupert: The harpsichord arrived from the country a semitone flat, and the tuner had gone home.
Hilde: The whole orchestra transposed. By sight. During the overture.
Rupert: Every string player. Every wind player. One key down, no rehearsal, no discussion.
Hilde: The oboe refused, and the oboe was right, because the oboe cannot.
Rupert: So the oboe sat out and has been insufferable ever since.
Hilde: For three hundred years. Here is the piece, in the key it was written in.

segments.flavor: Hilde corrects one date or key signature with love; Rupert accepts the correction like a plot twist
segments.text:
Rupert: The symphony arrived in seventeen eighty-seven, in a summer so hot the ink would not dry.
Hilde: Seventeen eighty-eight, Rupert. Not seven.
Rupert: Eighty-eight. Then he was a year poorer and the ink still would not dry.
Hilde: He wrote three symphonies that summer. Nobody paid him for any of them.
Rupert: Thrilling. Devastating. Here is the second of the three.

segments.flavor: a fake ad for hearing aids, velvet seats or a subscription series, hushed sincere announcer grammar, rapid disclaimer from Hilde
segments.text:
Rupert: Concert Hall thanks Softsole, the evening shoe for people who arrive during the first movement.
Hilde: The heel is felt. The sole is felt. The shame is left untreated.
Rupert: Softsole crosses an old wooden floor at a quarter of the usual volume.
Hilde: Softsole will not find your seat for you in the dark.
Rupert: Nothing will. Row nine, aisle side, and back to the strings.

segments.flavor: back-announce {STREAM} as tonight's orchestra, with one line of program notes
segments.text:
Rupert: That was tonight's orchestra, and that was a concerto written for a left hand alone.
Hilde: The right hand was lost in a war. The music never mentions it.
Rupert: You hear two hands. There is one. The thriller is in what is missing.
Hilde: The composer heard it once, and wept, and said nothing useful afterwards.
Rupert: Nobody ever does. More from the same orchestra now.

segments.flavor: Gus the night watchman weighs in on the last tempo; he thinks it rushed, and he has keys to find
segments.text:
Gus: Evening. Whoever conducted that finale was being chased by something.
Rupert: It is marked presto, Gus.
Gus: Presto is a speed. That was a getaway.
Hilde: [chuckle] He is not wrong. The last page is three bars shorter than the score.
Rupert: Gus, you have keys to find.
Gus: I have one left. It opens the organ loft, and I am in no hurry.
Hilde: Then take an adagio with you. Here it is.

segments.flavor: Rupert tells one ordinary biographical fact about a composer as a thriller — debts, deadlines, a chase — and lands on 'and then — silence'
segments.text:
Rupert: The bailiffs came at dawn. He had one symphony, unfinished, and a mattress.
Hilde: He put the symphony in the mattress.
Rupert: They took the chairs. They took the clock. They sat on the mattress to write the list.
Hilde: [gasp] On it?
Rupert: On it. Forty minutes. Then they left, and the symphony was still there.
Hilde: He finished it that week and sold it to pay for the chairs.
Rupert: And then — silence. Then the slow movement, which he wrote sitting on the floor.

segments.flavor: Hilde corrects one date or key signature with love; Rupert accepts the correction like a plot twist
segments.text:
Rupert: They call it The Hunt, because of the horns in the opening bars.
Hilde: The composer never called it anything. A publisher in Vienna called it The Hunt.
Rupert: So the horns are not horns.
Hilde: The horns are horns. The hunt is an invention, sold on the cover, in larger type.
Rupert: A publisher renamed a masterpiece to move copies. That is a heist.
Hilde: It is marketing, and it worked for two hundred years.
Rupert: Then let us hear the crime. Horns first.

segments.flavor: a fake ad for hearing aids, velvet seats or a subscription series, hushed sincere announcer grammar, rapid disclaimer from Hilde
segments.text:
Rupert: Concert Hall is brought to you by Cloakroom Nine, where your coat is returned warm.
Hilde: Warm. They keep the rail above the radiator.
Rupert: The radiator that plays B flat.
Hilde: Your coat comes back in tune. Some patrons report a faint hum in the lining.
Rupert: Cloakroom Nine. One ticket, one coat, no argument at the end of the evening.
Hilde: Cloakroom Nine is not responsible for what you left in the pockets.
Rupert: Nothing good, ever. The overture, now.

segments.flavor: Gus the night watchman weighs in on the last tempo; he thinks it rushed, and he has keys to find
segments.text:
Rupert: Gus is here, which means the last one was too fast.
Gus: The last one was fine. The one before it was a scandal.
Hilde: [surprised] Oh. A scandal.
Gus: Nobody needs to reach the end of a minuet that badly.
Rupert: The conductor is admired for his energy, Gus.
Hilde: He is also admired for finishing eight minutes early.
Gus: I walk the whole building after. Eleven doors. Energy is not the problem.
Rupert: Then we take the next one at your pace. Eleven doors, one adagio.

segments.flavor: Hilde corrects one date or key signature with love; Rupert accepts the correction like a plot twist
segments.text:
Rupert: He wrote it at midnight, by one candle, with the shutters closed against his creditors.
Hilde: He wrote it after breakfast. The household accounts say so, in his wife's hand.
Rupert: After breakfast.
Hilde: With the shutters open. There was a dog.
Rupert: You are taking the candle away from me, Hilde.
Hilde: I am giving you a dog and a window. It is a better scene.
Rupert: And the key is A minor.
Hilde: A flat major. With love, Rupert. A flat.
Rupert: A flat major, after breakfast, with a dog. The thriller survives.
Hilde: It always does. The music is the alibi.
Rupert: Then hear the alibi. Second movement first, because he wrote it first.

segments.flavor: a fake ad for hearing aids, velvet seats or a subscription series, hushed sincere announcer grammar, rapid disclaimer from Hilde
segments.text:
Rupert: [gentle] Concert Hall is supported by Hushwell, and Hushwell has added a room.
Hilde: A room?
Rupert: The Hall Setting. It adds the reverberation of a stone church to whatever you are hearing.
Hilde: Your kitchen becomes a cathedral. Your kettle becomes an event.
Rupert: The tap in the bathroom becomes a fountain in an Italian courtyard.
Hilde: The dog becomes a choir.
Rupert: Every Hushwell is fitted by a person who has heard an orchestra from the inside.
Hilde: The Hall Setting cannot be switched off during an argument, and we did warn you.
Rupert: We did. Hushwell. Hear the room that is not there.
Hilde: Now hear the one that is. The orchestra returns.

segments.flavor: back-announce {STREAM} as tonight's orchestra, with one line of program notes
segments.text:
Rupert: That was tonight's orchestra, and the piece was written for a funeral that was cancelled.
Hilde: The patron recovered. He lived another thirty years and never mentioned the music again.
Rupert: Imagine hearing your own funeral music at dinner. Twice.
Hilde: The score sat in a cupboard until his grandson sold the cupboard.
Rupert: The buyer wanted the cupboard. The music came free, in a drawer, under a hat.
Hilde: The hat is in a museum. The music is here.
Rupert: Which is the correct arrangement.
Hilde: The second subject is the one that sounds like a question.
Rupert: It is a question. Nobody answers it, which is why we keep playing it.
Hilde: Play it again, hat and all.

segments.flavor: Gus the night watchman weighs in on the last tempo; he thinks it rushed, and he has keys to find
segments.text:
Rupert: The watchman has arrived with an opinion and a face.
Gus: That overture was played by people who wanted to go home.
Hilde: They did want to go home. It was a long rehearsal.
Gus: Then they should have gone home. You do not hurry a beginning.
Rupert: Gus times the overtures against the clock in the east corridor.
Hilde: The clock is four minutes fast.
Rupert: The clock is the only honest thing in the building, according to Gus.
Hilde: The radiator is honest. It is a B flat, and it is holding.
Gus: The radiator never rushes. Forty years. Same note. Learn from the radiator.
Rupert: Words for the whole profession. Take your keys, Gus.
Hilde: And take us into something slow enough for him.

segments.flavor: a fake ad — Rowlight, a lamp for one page
segments.text:
Rupert: Rowlight is a lamp the size of a thumb, and it points at one page only.
Hilde: One page. Not the row. Not the stage. Not the soloist's music stand.
Rupert: The beam stops where the page stops. The person beside you stays in the dark.
Hilde: Where they belong.
Rupert: Rowlight runs for eleven hours, which is two operas and one interval.
Hilde: Rowlight is not a torch, a signal, or a way to find the exit.
Rupert: For that we have Gus. The next piece, please.

segments.flavor: a fake ad — the Movement Counter
segments.text:
Rupert: [gentle] The Movement Counter is a card, and the card knows how many movements remain.
Hilde: Four holes. One thumb. You move the thumb. The card tells the truth.
Rupert: No more clapping alone in a silent hall. No more the look from row A.
Hilde: The look from row A is a national treasure and should be preserved.
Rupert: The Movement Counter. Small, quiet, and correct.
Hilde: The Movement Counter does not work on an opera, a suite, or anything French.
Rupert: Nothing works on anything French. Count us back in.

segments.flavor: a fake ad — Crescendo Cellars, the interval wine
segments.text:
Rupert: Crescendo Cellars pours your interval wine before the first note is played.
Hilde: It waits on a small shelf with your name on a card.
Rupert: No queue. No elbows. No forty minutes of hope for one glass.
Hilde: The wine is warm by then.
Rupert: The wine is at the temperature of the room, which is the same sentence, said kindly.
Hilde: Crescendo Cellars is not responsible for the second half.
Rupert: Nobody is. Glasses down, and on we go.

segments.flavor: a fake ad — Tempus, the pocket metronome
segments.text:
Rupert: Tempus is a metronome the size of a coin, and it keeps your own time.
Hilde: Your own time is usually wrong. That is the charm of the product.
Rupert: Wind it once. It ticks for a week. It never apologises.
Hilde: It does not stop when you stop. It waits, and it judges.
Rupert: Tempus. For the student, the conductor, and the man with the keys.
Hilde: Tempus is not an argument, although it has ended several.
Rupert: It has. Set it aside, and let the orchestra decide.

segments.flavor: And Then — Silence — the bellows boy
segments.text:
Rupert: An organ needs air, and air needs a boy on a lever, and the boy was fourteen.
Hilde: He had been pumping since the morning service. It was now evening.
Rupert: In the middle of the fugue, the boy slept. The air ran out.
Hilde: The sound goes down like a ship. Slowly. Then not at all.
Rupert: Four hundred people heard a great fugue die of exhaustion.
Hilde: The organist kept his hands on the keys until the last of the air was gone.
Rupert: And then — silence. Real silence, the kind you can hear.
Hilde: The boy woke and pumped. They started again. We start again too.

segments.flavor: And Then — Silence — the score in the fish basket
segments.text:
Rupert: The only score was stolen on a Tuesday. The premiere was on the Friday.
Hilde: Stolen, or borrowed by a rival with a sense of theatre.
Rupert: The composer did not write it out again. He went to bed.
Hilde: [surprised] He went to bed?
Rupert: For two days. His housekeeper answered the door and told everyone he was dead.
Hilde: She was protecting him. She was also enjoying it.
Rupert: On Thursday evening a basket of fish arrived at the kitchen door.
Hilde: Under the fish, wrapped in cloth, the score. Dry. Complete. Unsigned.
Rupert: It smelled of the harbour for the rest of its life. It still does.
Hilde: The library keeps it in a box of its own, for that reason.
Rupert: Nobody ever confessed. Here is Friday.

segments.flavor: And Then — Silence — the wrong act
segments.text:
Rupert: She came on for act three. The orchestra was in act two.
Hilde: She had been waiting in a cold corridor for forty minutes, and she had had enough.
Rupert: She sang the aria from the last act, at the wrong end of the story.
Hilde: The conductor had one second to choose, and he chose her.
Rupert: The orchestra turned twenty pages at once. It sounded like a flock of birds.
Hilde: Then they played the last act, then the second, then the third.
Rupert: The opera ended in the middle. The audience stood up anyway.
Hilde: Two critics called it a revelation. One of them knew what had happened.
Rupert: The other has a chair at a university.
Hilde: [chuckle] He does.
Rupert: Wrong order, right music. That is our whole programme, honestly.
Hilde: It is. Take us out with her aria, in its proper place.

segments.flavor: And Then — Silence — the duel over a bowing mark
segments.text:
Rupert: Two violinists disagreed about one bowing mark. Up, or down.
Hilde: Up or down. Three strokes of a pen, and they went outside.
Rupert: Swords, at dawn, behind the theatre, over the direction of a bow.
Hilde: Neither was hurt. Both were cold. Both were sorry by breakfast.
Rupert: They played the concert that evening, side by side, at the same desk.
Hilde: And the bowing in the parts is still ambiguous, because neither would mark it.
Rupert: Every orchestra since has argued about that bar.
Hilde: Politely. Mostly.
Rupert: Listen to the bar. You will not hear the duel, and that is the tragedy.
Hilde: Play on.
